fields.title: Razvoz: Demand Doubled, Supply Remained Unchanged
fields.summary: The city doubles in volume, requests hang for 24 hours, rating drops. Decide what to do over six weeks.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do over six weeks?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of the core marketplace team.
fields.brief/company: Razvoz is a fictional marketplace connecting people with vetted home repair specialists across 14 cities.
fields.brief/context: Samara was the third city and performed well for two years. Over the last four months, a successful feature in a local publication and a referral program roughly doubled demand there. Supply — the number of active specialists — grew by 11%. Time to acceptance increased from 40 minutes to 4 hours, 23% of requests sit unaccepted for 24 hours, and rating dropped from 4.7 to 4.3. The growth team wants to keep spending: customer acquisition cost in Samara is three times lower than the network average.
fields.brief/objective: Restore city health without losing what was built.
fields.brief/constraints: Four developers and one operations coordinator assigned to Samara, up to six weeks. Specialist acquisition is handled by another team with its own goals. Price changes require approval.
fields.brief/task: Choose what to do and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Cheap demand stops being cheap when no one is there to serve it
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Acquisition cost three times lower than the network average is a strong argument only as long as the acquired user returns. After waiting 24 hours, they do not return in two out of three cases, turning all savings into a loss. In a marketplace, growth is not validated on one side alone: if load on supply grows faster than supply itself, you must throttle demand, even when it is the cheapest in the company.
fields.evidenceCards/0/title: What is happening in the city
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Nine interviews with Samara specialists, including three who recently stopped accepting requests.

All nine called the request feed "noisy". Several said they used to check twice a day, but now "it is a flood, and most of it is not worth the time".

The three who left cited one reason — small jobs: "You scroll through forty requests for eight hundred rubles to find one worth driving to".

Two of them continue working through another platform where, in their words, "you only see what fits me".

None of the nine complained about the commission fee.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Customer acquisition cost in Samara is 340 ₽, network average is 920 ₽. The referral promo brings roughly 60% of new demand, the publication brought most of the rest.

Customers whose request hung for 24 hours: 61% do not place another request within 90 days.
Customers whose request was accepted within an hour: 34% place another request.

Commission is 12% of the job value, identical for everyone.

Average request value in Samara dropped from 4,100 ₽ to 2,600 ₽: the promo brought many small jobs.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What can be done in six weeks
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Estimates for changes that can be rolled out in Samara:

— Filters and feed relevance: specialist filters by job value, distance, and job type; feed is ranked by relevance rather than recency. Three weeks. Then rolled out network-wide.
— Notifications for matching requests: one week, depends on relevance.
— Minimum order value or surcharge on small orders: two weeks plus pricing approval.
— Grouping small requests into a route: five weeks, never tested.

Pausing the referral promo takes one day; decision rests with the growth team.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Make feed relevant and pause the promotion
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Three weeks for filters and relevance ranking, while pausing the referral promo in Samara immediately to stop pouring in demand that no one can serve.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Pausing the promo takes one day and cuts 60% of new demand — the cheapest demand bringing the smallest requests that made the feed noisy.
This is uncomfortable for the growth team: 340 ₽ versus 920 ₽ network-wide looks like the best deal in the company. The argument that works: a customer whose request hangs for 24 hours does not return in 61% of cases — meaning we pay 340 ₽ for a customer and lose them.
In three weeks, filters and relevance ranking ship. Specialists stop scrolling forty small requests: accepted jobs per specialist return to 3.1 per week, time to acceptance drops to 55 minutes, unaccepted share to 7%.
Specialist churn returns to 8%, rating rises to 4.6 within a month.
The work is rolled out to the remaining 13 cities — it is needed wherever demand grows.
Trade-off: the city grows slower than it could, and the growth team's Samara goal for this quarter is missed.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Introduce a minimum request value or a surcharge for small requests in Samara, so that eight-hundred-ruble jobs either become economical or stop appearing.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Two weeks of work plus pricing approval — fits within the timeline.
There is an effect: the share of small requests drops, the feed becomes cleaner, time to acceptance shrinks to 1.5 hours.
However, part of demand simply vanishes: customers with 800 ₽ requests leave, and those are the exact people acquired for 340 ₽. Average order value grows, request volume drops by a third.
Specialists who complained about noise are satisfied; the three who left do not return — they needed visibility into relevant jobs, not higher prices.
Trade-off: the feed problem is solved by cutting off a demand segment, even though none of the nine specialists complained about commissions.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Solve small order economics via product: group three nearby requests into a single route so they become profitable to take.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
An elegant idea that was never tested; estimate is five weeks out of the available six.
After five weeks, the first version ships, and it turns out specialists take a route only if all three requests are in the same neighborhood and same job type — few such combinations exist in the feed.
During this time, the feed remains noisy, specialist churn holds at 14%, and the promo keeps pouring in demand.
By the end of week six, you have an unproven mechanic and a city in the exact same state.
Trade-off: the most expensive and unproven bet was chosen over a viable three-week alternative.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Keep spending and push specialist acquisition
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Acquisition cost in Samara is 340 ₽ versus 920 ₽ network-wide. Maintain demand and ask the supply team to recruit more specialists.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The supply team accepts the task, but they have their own quarterly goals: recruiting specialists in a single city moves slowly, adding 40 people in six weeks against doubled demand.
Time to acceptance keeps growing, the share of requests unaccepted for 24 hours reaches 29%, rating falls to 4.1.
Specialist churn accelerates: 14% turns into 19% because feed noise worsens.
Customers acquired for 340 ₽ leave in 61% of cases after waiting 24 hours, turning cheap acquisition into an expensive loss.
Trade-off: preserved the most attractive metric in the report at the expense of what it was measured for.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Goal is framed as work rather than outcome and fulfilled by shipping a feature
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Strategy does not state where we do not play and what we choose to give up
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Identical requirements are applied to all products in the portfolio
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Vision does not rule out a single good idea, meaning it does not work
